Overlap avoids splitting a fact across chunks
Chose by measuring retrieval quality (e.g. recall@k) on a labelled set

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In your support-bot project, how did you choose the chunk size for retrieval?

transcript.speaker: candidate
transcript.text: We started with 256, 512 and 1024 token chunks with a 50 token overlap, because our docs were support articles where one answer often spans two paragraphs. I built a labelled set of 120 real tickets mapped to the article section that answers them and measured recall at 5. 512 gave 0.83 versus 0.71 for 256, because small chunks cut the explanation away from the keyword. 1024 had similar recall but doubled the prompt tokens and the model got distracted by unrelated text, so faithfulness dropped. So we picked 512 with overlap, and we re-run that eval whenever we change the embedding model.

notes: A complete, specific, correct answer must score well.

question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate on a technical decision.
ideal_key_points: Specific situation with context and stakes
Their own actions: how they raised and argued the disagreement
How it was resolved, ideally with data or an experiment
Concrete result and what they learned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate on a technical decision.

transcript.speaker: candidate
transcript.text: On our document QA project my teammate wanted to fine-tune a model, and I thought RAG was enough, because our documents changed every week. I didn't want it to become an opinion fight, so I proposed a two-day spike: I built a small RAG baseline and we both agreed on a 30-question eval set first. RAG scored 78 percent correct against 64 for the fine-tuned model, at a fraction of the cost, and updates were instant. We shipped RAG, and my teammate later used fine-tuning just for the tone of the answers. I learned to agree on the metric before arguing about the solution.

notes: Clear STAR with personal actions and a measured result.
